opus-5.5.text:
I'd push back a little on the framing first: whether something is a bubble depends on whether valuations are running ahead of what the technology can actually deliver within a reasonable time. My sense is that in embodied intelligence the gap is smaller than people assume, and here's why.

First, the underlying capability shift is real. For decades, robotics was hand-engineered: you programmed every motion and every edge case, and the robot fell apart the moment the environment changed. What's different now is that large models have given robots a kind of general prior, a way to understand language, scenes, and intent. Combined with learning-based control, we're seeing robots handle tasks no one explicitly programmed. That isn't a demo trick. It's a change in how the whole stack is built.

Second, the hardware supply chain is maturing fast, especially in China. Motors, reducers, sensors, batteries: costs have dropped dramatically over the past few years because of the EV and consumer electronics industries. A humanoid or mobile manipulator that would have cost several hundred thousand dollars not long ago is getting into a range where real commercial deployment starts to make sense. A bubble usually means there's no path to unit economics. Here, the path is visible, even if we're not there yet.

Third, the demand side is structural. Aging populations and labor shortages in manufacturing, logistics, and elder care aren't hype cycles. They're demographic facts. Even if general-purpose humanoids take longer than the optimists say, there's a lot of value in narrower embodied systems along the way.

That said, I won't pretend everything is rational. Some companies are raising money on videos rather than deployments, and some valuations price in a timeline that I think is too aggressive. Data is still the biggest bottleneck. We don't have an internet-scale dataset for physical interaction, and nobody has fully solved how to get one. So there will be a shakeout. Some teams won't survive.

But a shakeout isn't the same as a bubble. The internet had a crash in 2000, and the internet was still the most important technology of the next twenty years. I'd say embodied intelligence is early, noisy, and probably overfunded in places, but the core direction is sound. The real question isn't whether it's a bubble. It's who can turn capability into reliable deployment fastest.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I'd push back a little on the framing first. I don't think the question is whether there's a bubble — there's always some froth whenever capital rushes into a new direction, and anyone who tells you there's zero froth in embodied intelligence right now isn't being straight with you. The real question is whether the underlying thing is real. And on that I'm quite confident: it is.

Let me give you a few reasons.

The first is that the technical foundation has genuinely changed. Five years ago, if you wanted a robot to do a new task, you basically had to program it from scratch — write the trajectories, tune the controllers, build the perception pipeline for that one environment. Every deployment was a bespoke engineering project. What large models did was give us a way to transfer general capability. Language understanding, visual understanding, some amount of commonsense reasoning — these now come for free, more or less. So the robot no longer starts from zero. That's a qualitative shift, not an incremental one, and it's the reason so many people who spent decades in robotics and had basically given up on general-purpose machines suddenly got excited again.

The second reason is demand. A bubble, to me, is when valuations run far ahead of any plausible use. But the demand side here is not speculative — it's structural. Look at manufacturing in China, look at logistics, look at elder care in Japan and increasingly here. Labor costs keep rising, the working-age population is shrinking, and factories are already struggling to hire for the repetitive, physically demanding jobs. That's not a story someone invented to justify a funding round. That's demographics. So even if the technology arrives slower than the optimists hope, there's a buyer waiting at the end.

Third — and this is the part people in Silicon Valley sometimes underestimate — the supply chain is here. Motors, reducers, sensors, batteries, the whole hardware stack. China built it for EVs and consumer electronics, and it turns out most of it transfers directly. That means the cost of iterating on hardware is much lower than it was even three or four years ago. A startup can build a humanoid prototype for a fraction of what Boston Dynamics spent. When the iteration cost drops that much, you get a lot of experiments, and some fraction of them will work.

Now, where I'd be careful. Will most of the companies raising money today survive? No. Probably not. The majority won't. Some of the valuations are detached from any revenue timeline I can see, and a lot of the demos you see online are heavily cherry-picked — one successful run out of twenty, teleoperated when nobody's looking. I'm not naive about that.

But that's actually how every important technology wave has looked. The internet in 1999 had a bubble, and it was also obviously the future. Both things were true at once. The bubble was in who gets the value and how fast, not in whether the thing matters. I think embodied intelligence is the same. The mistake would be to look at the froth and conclude the direction is wrong.

So my short answer: there's a bubble in valuations, maybe. There's no bubble in the problem. And the problem is what you should be betting on.

astra-6.text:
I’d distinguish between enthusiasm around investment and whether the industry itself is a bubble. Some companies may be overvalued, and some expectations may be running ahead of what the technology can deliver. But that doesn’t mean the underlying demand is imaginary.

The need for machines that can do useful work in the physical world is real—in manufacturing, logistics, and other settings where tasks are repetitive, demanding, or difficult to staff. The question is whether embodied intelligence can meet those needs reliably and at an acceptable cost.

So I wouldn’t judge the industry by how impressive a demonstration looks, or how much funding a company raises. I’d look at whether a robot can keep working in a real environment, how often someone has to intervene, and whether the customer gets enough value to pay for it again.

That’s why I don’t think calling the whole industry a bubble is particularly helpful. There can be speculative investment around a real technological opportunity. The opportunity is substantial, but turning it into a business still requires proving reliability, usefulness, and economics.

sol-6.1.text:
I think we need to distinguish between high expectations and a bubble. Embodied intelligence certainly attracts a lot of excitement, and some companies may be overvalued. But that doesn’t mean the entire industry is a bubble.

The underlying demand is real. There are physical tasks that people want machines to perform because they’re repetitive, dangerous, or difficult to staff. The question is whether a robot can perform those tasks reliably and at a cost that makes sense.

For me, that’s the test: can you move beyond a demonstration, deploy in a real environment, and create enough value that a customer wants to keep paying? A compelling video isn’t enough. You have to account for failures, maintenance, and how much human intervention the system needs.

So I wouldn’t say there’s no speculation. There can be speculative valuations within an industry that has a real future. I think the opportunity is substantial, but companies still have to prove it through actual use.
